q: Rectification is the process of:
o: Converting alternating current into direct current
Converting direct current into alternating current
Increasing the voltage of an alternating supply
x: A rectifier changes AC into (pulsating) DC by allowing current through the load in one direction only. Changing DC to AC is inversion; increasing AC voltage is done by a transformer.

q: The number of diodes used in a simple half-wave rectifier is:
x: A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode in series with the load. Two diodes are used in a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier and four in a bridge rectifier.

q: In a half-wave rectifier, current flows through the load resistor:
o: During both halves of each input cycle
Only at the peak of the input voltage
During only one half of each input cycle
x: The diode conducts only when it is forward biased, which happens in one half-cycle; in the other half-cycle it is reverse biased and blocks the current.

q: A half-wave rectifier is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. The frequency of the output pulses is:
x: One half-cycle per input cycle is passed, so there is one output pulse per cycle: 50 pulses per second, the same as the input frequency.

q: A full-wave rectifier is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. The frequency of the output pulses is:
x: Both half-cycles give an output pulse, so there are 2 pulses per input cycle: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

q: The number of diodes in a bridge rectifier is:
x: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged in a bridge, so it gives full-wave rectification without a centre-tapped transformer.

q: In a bridge rectifier, during each half-cycle of the input, the number of diodes conducting is:
x: In each half-cycle one pair of opposite diodes is forward biased and conducts in series through the load; the other pair is reverse biased.

q: The main advantage of a full-wave rectifier over a half-wave rectifier is that it:
o: Uses both halves of the input cycle, giving a larger and smoother output
Gives a perfectly steady DC output without any filter
Converts DC into AC as well
x: A full-wave rectifier uses both half-cycles, so no half of the input is wasted and the output pulses come twice as often. It needs more diodes, and its output is still pulsating DC.

q: Without a filter, the output of a rectifier is:
x: The output flows in one direction but its size rises and falls with the input, so it is unidirectional pulsating DC.

q: The output of a full-wave rectifier has 200 pulses per second. The frequency of the AC input is:
x: A full-wave rectifier gives 2 pulses per input cycle, so input frequency = 200/2 = 100 Hz. 400 Hz comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

q: A full-wave rectifier using only two diodes requires:
o: A battery in series with the load
A transformer with a centre-tapped secondary
x: In the two-diode full-wave rectifier, each diode conducts in turn through half of a centre-tapped secondary coil. The bridge rectifier, with four diodes, avoids the centre tap.

q: In a full-wave rectifier, the current through the load resistor during the two halves of the input cycle flows:
o: In the same direction in both halves
In opposite directions in the two halves
In the same direction but only at the peaks
x: The diodes are arranged so that in both half-cycles the current passes through the load in the same direction; this is what makes the output DC.

q: In a bridge rectifier one diode becomes open-circuited (stops conducting completely). The circuit now:
o: Still works as a full-wave rectifier
x: The diode pair containing the broken diode can no longer complete its path, so that half-cycle gives no output. The other pair still conducts in its half-cycle, giving half-wave rectification.

q: The depletion region of a PN junction contains:
o: A large number of free electrons only
A large number of free holes only
Immobile positive and negative ions, with almost no free charge carriers
Equal numbers of free electrons and holes moving freely
x: Electrons and holes near the junction recombine, leaving fixed (immobile) donor and acceptor ions; the region is 'depleted' of mobile charge carriers.

q: The potential barrier of a silicon PN junction is about:
x: For silicon the barrier potential is about 0.7 V; about 0.3 V is the value for germanium.

q: A PN junction is forward biased when:
o: The p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal
Both sides are connected to the positive terminal
The p-side is connected to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative terminal
x: In forward bias the positive terminal pushes holes from the p-side, and the negative terminal pushes electrons from the n-side, towards the junction.

q: When a PN junction is forward biased, its depletion region:
o: Becomes wider and the potential barrier is increased
Disappears completely at any applied voltage
Becomes narrower and the potential barrier is reduced
x: The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, so the depletion region narrows and majority carriers can cross; once the applied voltage exceeds the barrier, current rises sharply.

q: When a PN junction is reverse biased:
o: The depletion region narrows and a large current flows
The barrier potential falls to zero
Majority carriers flow easily across the junction
The depletion region widens and only a very small current flows
x: Reverse bias adds to the barrier, so the depletion region widens and majority carriers cannot cross; only a tiny leakage current due to minority carriers flows.

q: The depletion region forms at a PN junction because:
o: A battery must be connected to create it
Electrons diffuse from the n-side and holes from the p-side across the junction and recombine
Electrons flow from the p-side to the n-side
The p-type material has more free electrons than the n-type
x: With no battery, electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n; they recombine near the junction, leaving behind a layer of fixed ions that sets up the barrier.

q: In the depletion region of an unbiased PN junction, the p-side and the n-side carry respectively:
x: The p-side loses holes and keeps fixed negative acceptor ions; the n-side loses electrons and keeps fixed positive donor ions.

q: A light-emitting diode (LED) gives out light when it is:
o: Reverse biased, so the depletion region widens
Forward biased, so electrons and holes recombine at the junction
Reverse biased beyond its breakdown voltage
x: In forward bias, electrons cross into the p-side and recombine with holes; the energy released in each recombination leaves as a photon. Reverse bias stops the current, so there is no recombination and no light.

q: A photodiode is normally operated in reverse bias. When the intensity of light falling on its junction is increased, its reverse current:
o: Increases, because more electron-hole pairs are produced
Decreases, because the depletion region widens
Stays the same, because reverse current depends only on temperature
x: Photons absorbed in the depletion region create electron-hole pairs, which the reverse-bias field sweeps across, so the reverse current rises with light intensity. The tempting slip is to think reverse bias always means no current; here light supplies the minority carriers.

q: An LED that drops 2 V when lit is connected in series with a resistor across a 6 V battery. What resistance makes the LED current 20 mA?
x: The resistor takes 6 − 2 = 4 V, so R = V/I = 4/0.020 = 200 Ω. Using the full 6 V gives 300 Ω, using the LED's 2 V gives 100 Ω, and forgetting to change 20 mA to 0.020 A gives 0.2 Ω.

q: Each photon emitted by an LED carries 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J of energy. What is the wavelength of its light? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: λ = hc/E = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.6 × 10⁻⁷ m = 660 nm (red light). The other options come from a power-of-ten slip when changing metres to nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m).

q: A solar cell of area 0.01 m² is placed in sunlight of intensity 1000 W m⁻². It delivers 1.5 W of electrical power to a load. What is its efficiency?
x: Input power = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 W, so efficiency = 1.5/10 × 100 % = 15 %. Dividing input by output (10/1.5) gives 6.7 %, and losing a factor of 10 in the area gives 1.5 %.

q: For a transistor with emitter current I_E, base current I_B and collector current I_C, the correct relation is:
x: Charge entering at the emitter divides between base and collector, so I_E = I_B + I_C. The emitter current is the largest of the three; the base current is a small fraction of it.

q: A transistor has a current gain β = 100. If its base current is 20 μA, its collector current is:
x: I_C = β I_B = 100 × 20 μA = 2000 μA = 2 mA. The value 2.02 mA is the emitter current (I_B + I_C), and 0.2 mA or 20 mA come from a slip converting μA to mA.

q: In a transistor the emitter current is 5.00 mA and the collector current is 4.95 mA. What is the current gain β = I_C/I_B?
x: I_B = I_E − I_C = 5.00 − 4.95 = 0.05 mA, so β = 4.95/0.05 = 99. Dividing I_E by I_B gives 100, and I_C/I_E gives 0.99, which is the common-base ratio, not β.

q: For a transistor to work as an amplifier, its base-emitter junction and its base-collector junction must be, respectively:
x: Forward bias on the base-emitter junction lets carriers enter the base; reverse bias on the base-collector junction collects them, giving the active region needed for amplification. Both reverse biased is the cut-off (switch OFF) state, and both forward biased is saturation (switch ON).

q: A common-emitter amplifier uses a transistor with β = 50, a collector resistor of 4 kΩ and an input resistance of 1 kΩ. An input signal of 10 mV is applied. What is the size of the output signal?
x: Voltage gain magnitude = βR_C/r_ie = 50 × 4 kΩ/1 kΩ = 200, so output = 200 × 10 mV = 2000 mV = 2 V (inverted in phase). Using β alone gives 0.5 V, and using R_C/r_ie alone gives 0.04 V.

q: An inverting amplifier uses an op-amp with input resistor R₁ and feedback resistor R₂. Its voltage gain is:
x: For the inverting amplifier, gain = −R₂/R₁: the size is set by the feedback-to-input ratio and the minus sign shows the output is inverted. 1 + R₂/R₁ is the gain of the non-inverting amplifier.

q: An inverting op-amp amplifier has an input resistor of 10 kΩ and a feedback resistor of 100 kΩ. If the input voltage is +0.2 V, the output voltage is:
x: Gain = −R_f/R_in = −100/10 = −10, so V_out = −10 × 0.2 = −2 V. Forgetting the inversion gives +2 V, and using the non-inverting formula 1 + R_f/R_in = 11 gives 2.2 V.

q: In a non-inverting op-amp amplifier, the resistor from the inverting input to earth is 2 kΩ and the feedback resistor is 18 kΩ. An input of 0.3 V gives an output of:
x: Gain = 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + 18/2 = 10, so V_out = 10 × 0.3 = 3 V, in phase with the input. Using R_f/R₁ = 9 gives 2.7 V; the negative values come from using the inverting-amplifier sign.

q: An op-amp powered from ±12 V is used as a comparator without feedback. Its non-inverting input is held at 2 V and a signal of 3 V is applied to its inverting input. The output is:
x: V_out = A(V₊ − V₋) = A(2 − 3) with a huge open-loop gain A, so the output swings to negative saturation, close to −12 V. The tempting −1 V forgets the enormous gain; +12 V reverses the inputs.

q: In an inverting amplifier built with an ideal op-amp, the non-inverting input is earthed. While the amplifier is working normally, the potential of the inverting input is about:
o: Equal to the positive supply voltage
x: With very large open-loop gain and negative feedback, V₋ is driven to nearly equal V₊ = 0 V, so the inverting input is a virtual earth. This is why the current through R₁ is V_in/R₁, giving gain −R₂/R₁.

q: The output of a two-input NOR gate is 1:
o: When at least one input is 1
When the two inputs are different
x: NOR is OR followed by NOT. OR gives 0 only when both inputs are 0, so NOR gives 1 only in that case. 'Both inputs 1' describes AND; 'inputs different' describes XOR.

q: A two-input logic gate gives an output of 1 when its two inputs are different and 0 when they are the same. The gate is:
x: Exclusive-OR outputs 1 for inputs 0,1 and 1,0 and outputs 0 for 0,0 and 1,1. XNOR is the reverse; OR also gives 1 for 1,1, which is the usual slip.

q: Both inputs of a two-input NAND gate are joined together and fed with the same signal P. The gate now behaves as:
o: A buffer whose output equals P
x: With both inputs equal to P, NAND gives NOT(P·P) = NOT P: P = 0 gives 1 and P = 1 gives 0. Forgetting the inversion would make it look like an AND gate or a buffer.

q: Signal P is fed to one input of an OR gate, and the same signal passed through a NOT gate is fed to the other input. The output of the OR gate is:
x: One of P and NOT P is always 1, so the OR output is P + P̄ = 1 for both P = 0 and P = 1. Feeding the same pair to an AND gate would always give 0, the tempting mix-up.

q: Inputs P and Q are fed to an AND gate and also to an OR gate. The two gate outputs are then fed to a two-input XOR gate. The final output is 1:
o: Only when P and Q are both 1
Only when P and Q are different
Only when P and Q are both 0
x: AND and OR outputs: 0,0 → 0 and 0; 0,1 → 0 and 1; 1,0 → 0 and 1; 1,1 → 1 and 1. XOR is 1 only when these differ, which happens for 0,1 and 1,0, so the circuit acts as an XOR of P and Q.
